lessons.title: Structural pattern matching
lessons.summary: Implement route(command) with match/case. ["greet", name] returns "Hello " plus name only when name is a string; ["pause"] returns "Paused"; everything else returns "Unknown". Accept matching tuples too and preserve input.
explanation: match command examines a value; each case is a pattern, not a function call. The sequence pattern ["greet", name] requires two elements, matches the literal first element, and binds the second to name. A bare name in a pattern captures a value; it does not compare against an earlier variable of that name.

The guard if isinstance(name, str) runs after the shape matches. isinstance receives a value and a class and returns a Boolean; here it rejects a non-string name. Only the first successful case runs. The wildcard _ matches anything without binding a new name, so put the fallback last.

```python
def route(command):
    match command:
        case ["greet", name] if isinstance(name, str):
            return f"Hello {name}"
        case ["pause"]:
            return "Paused"
        case _:
            return "Unknown"

print(route(["greet", "Ada"]))
print(route(["pause"]))
print(route(["greet", 7]))
```
The outputs are Hello Ada, Paused, and Unknown. route accepts a command value and returns one message string; it does not change the input.

Sequence patterns also match suitable tuples, but do not split str or bytes into characters. An extra element prevents this exact two-element pattern from matching. For example, route(["greet", "Ada", "extra"]) returns Unknown. Guard failure permits the following cases to be tried.

Implement route with the same three cases. Preserve a string name exactly, including spaces and non-English letters. The optional local transfer is to add a separate literal ["resume"] case before the wildcard and explain why its position matters.

lessons.title: Unicode text and UTF-8 bytes
lessons.summary: Write utf8_summary(text). Encode the supplied valid Unicode string as UTF-8 and return (byte_count, decoded_text). Preserve exact text without normalization; empty text returns (0, "").
explanation: str stores Unicode text; bytes stores byte values. len on a string counts Unicode code points, not necessarily visible grapheme clusters. len on bytes counts bytes. One visible character may contain several code points, and one code point may need several UTF-8 bytes.

text.encode("utf-8") takes an encoding name and returns new bytes representing the string. encoded.decode("utf-8") interprets bytes using that encoding and returns new text. Neither call edits the original object. The dot selects the method, and parentheses pass its encoding argument.

```python
text = "é"
encoded = text.encode("utf-8")
print(len(text))
print(len(encoded))
print(encoded.decode("utf-8"))
```
It prints 1, then 2, then é. The encoding changes representation rather than the meaning of the text.

Strict decoding is the default. b"\xff" is a one-byte literal written with a hexadecimal escape; it is not valid UTF-8. This complete example handles its specific failure:
```python
try:
    b"\xff".decode("utf-8")
except UnicodeDecodeError:
    print("Invalid UTF-8")
```
It prints Invalid UTF-8. Silently ignoring malformed bytes would lose information; choose a replacement policy only when the application explicitly permits it.

```python
def utf8_summary(text):
    encoded = text.encode("utf-8")
    return len(encoded), encoded.decode("utf-8")
print(utf8_summary("Café"))
```
It returns and prints (5, 'Café'): the byte count and exact round-tripped string. The project accepts ordinary Unicode strings encodable in UTF-8, not isolated surrogate code points. Optional local transfer: compare "é" with "e\u0301"; the two can look alike without being the same code-point sequence.

lessons.title: Floating-point closeness
lessons.summary: Implement close_readings(a, b) for finite real-number inputs using math.isclose with rel_tol=1e-6 and abs_tol=1e-9. Return the Boolean result, without rounding or modifying inputs.
explanation: 0.1 and 0.2 are not stored as exact decimal fractions in an ordinary float. Their sum can differ slightly from 0.3. This does not make every equality test wrong; choose exact or approximate comparison according to the contract.

math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=..., abs_tol=...) returns a Boolean. Relative tolerance scales with the larger absolute input magnitude; absolute tolerance permits a fixed maximum gap, important near zero. The comparison accepts a gap no larger than the greater of these allowances. Use nonnegative tolerances and a relative tolerance below 1 so the comparison represents a meaningful small-error policy.

```python
import math
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=0.0))
print(math.isclose(1e-12, 0.0, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9))
```
The outputs are False, True, True. import math makes the standard module available; the dot selects isclose. 1e-9 means one billionth. Named arguments keep the two policies explicit.

With one input zero and a relative tolerance below one, a nonzero other input cannot pass by relative tolerance alone. Changing the last abs_tol to 0.0 therefore gives False. A tolerance is an application decision, not a measured confidence interval or a repair for incorrect units.

```python
import math

def close_readings(a, b):
    return math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-6, abs_tol=1e-9)
print(close_readings(100.0, 100.00005))
print(close_readings(0.0, 1e-10))
print(close_readings(1.0, 1.01))
```
These calls return True, True, False. The project accepts finite real numbers; deciding what NaN or infinity means is outside that contract. Optional local transfer: pick different units and explain how the absolute tolerance would need to change.

lessons.title: Main guard and import effects
lessons.summary: Use supplied greeting_tool.py. Import it without calling its demonstration and implement personal_greeting(name) by returning greeting_tool.greeting(name). The program must print nothing on loading; the function preserves the supplied string name. The companion illustrates the main guard, and separate direct/import fixtures verify its two modes.
explanation: When a file is run as the top-level program, its __name__ is "__main__". When imported normally as greeting_tool, its __name__ is "greeting_tool". These are strings set by the execution context, not names you should manually overwrite.

Place this main.py beside greeting_tool.py:
```python
import greeting_tool
print(greeting_tool.greeting("Ada"))
```
It prints only Hello Ada. Import makes the definitions available but the guard skips the demonstration. Running python greeting_tool.py directly prints Hello Reader instead. Import still executes other unguarded top-level statements; the guard is not a blanket no-side-effects guarantee.

```python
import greeting_tool
greeting_tool.main()
```
It prints Hello Reader because you explicitly called main. The guard controls an automatic call during loading, not whether main may ever be called. This two-file example needs the supplied companion file; a single pasted import cannot create it.

Here is a complete wrapper call using the same companion:
```python
import greeting_tool
def personal_greeting(name):
    return greeting_tool.greeting(name)
print(personal_greeting("Ada"))
```
It prints Hello Ada. In the editor, complete the main-program caller: import the supplied greeting_tool and define personal_greeting(name) to return greeting_tool.greeting(name). Do not print or call main during this import/use exercise. Native and browser fixtures separately check the companion’s guarded behavior. Optional local transfer: run the companion directly, then run the importing main.py and compare the output.

lessons.title: Inheritance and super
lessons.summary: Complete Label and FramedLabel. Label(text) stores text and render() returns it. FramedLabel inherits the initializer; its render returns the base render result inside square brackets using super(). Preserve the stored text and independent instances.
explanation: class FramedLabel(Label) makes Label a base class. FramedLabel inherits its initializer and can replace render with its own implementation. Creating FramedLabel("Map") therefore still initializes self.text on that new instance.

Inside the overriding render method, super() returns a proxy for continuing method lookup after the current class. Calling .render() on that proxy reaches Label.render in this single-inheritance example, with the same instance. It is not a new Label object and does not mean "call every parent".

Replacing super().render() with self.render() inside FramedLabel.render calls that same overriding method again. With no stopping condition, it eventually raises RecursionError rather than reaching the base implementation.

Keep the base initializer and render method, and complete FramedLabel.render using super. Optional local transfer: make a second subclass with a different outer decoration and confirm neither changes the base object’s output.

lessons.title: Managed attributes with property
lessons.summary: Implement Duration(minutes) with a minutes property. Numeric nonnegative values are accepted; negative initialization or assignment raises ValueError before changing stored state. Getter returns the current numeric value. Keep the supplied test helper unchanged.
explanation: @property decorates the getter function so duration.minutes calls that getter through attribute syntax; callers do not write duration.minutes(). The getter returns the current stored value. A leading underscore in _minutes marks an internal convention, not enforced security.

@minutes.setter adds a setter to that same named property. Assignment duration.minutes = value invokes the setter with the receiver and new value. Here it checks the value before storing it in _minutes. Raising ValueError rejects a negative value without changing the old state; a property setter does not supply an assignment return value to the caller.

The getter reads self._minutes, not self.minutes. Reading self.minutes inside its own getter would re-enter the property recursively. The setter similarly stores the backing attribute instead of assigning the managed name again.

Complete the property with numeric nonnegative minutes. The supplied test helpers attempt a known invalid initialization and assignment; __rejects_negative checks that ValueError leaves the prior value intact; it is test infrastructure, not a general input evaluator. Optional local transfer: add a second explicit validation boundary, then show a successful and rejected assignment.

lessons.title: Class and static methods
lessons.summary: Complete Session.from_minutes as a class method returning cls("Study", minutes), and Session.valid_minutes as a static method returning minutes >= 0. Preserve the provided initializer and SpecialSession subclass. Factory inputs are nonnegative numeric values; the predicate also checks negative numeric values.
explanation: @classmethod changes method binding: the first argument, conventionally cls, receives the class used for the call, not an instance. from_minutes takes a number and returns cls("Study", minutes), creating the appropriate class through its constructor.

@staticmethod leaves valid_minutes as a function stored on the class: it receives only the explicit minutes argument and returns whether it is nonnegative. It does not automatically receive self or cls. This predicate checks a value; it does not modify or validate already constructed sessions by itself.

Replacing cls("Study", minutes) with Session("Study", minutes) always constructs the base class, even when called through SpecialSession. A factory using cls preserves the receiving subclass when its constructor has the compatible argument contract.

Implement the methods exactly as shown by their contracts. from_minutes accepts supplied nonnegative numeric minutes; valid_minutes separately reports a Boolean for numeric inputs. Optional local transfer: call the static predicate through a Session instance and explain why no receiver argument is added.
